summary: This informational document describes how Deterministic Networking (DetNet) traffic carried over MPLS runs across an IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) sub-network. It defines no new procedures. It collects statements that already appear in other RFCs and applies them to this combination, so implementers can see how flows map onto the TSN portion of the path.

plainLanguage.summary: Some data, like a robot arm's commands, must arrive on time every time. This document explains how to send such must-be-on-time messages over a special network that works like a train with a strict timetable.

questions: how does detnet run over time-sensitive networking
how does detnet work over tsn
what is the difference between a tsn-aware and tsn-unaware node
how do you map mpls flows to tsn streams
subtitle: How to run time-critical MPLS networks over reliable switching hardware.

tldr.problem: Networks that carry time-critical traffic (like industrial robots or real-time manufacturing) need to guarantee both fast and on-time delivery. Existing technologies don't fully address how to combine deterministic networking (DetNet) over MPLS with the guarantees offered by IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies how MPLS-based DetNet flows map to TSN streams, reusing existing protocols and techniques from both standards to provide low loss and bounded latency across a bridged network.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now construct end-to-end deterministic paths that combine MPLS routing control with TSN reliability and timing guarantees in the bridged portion of the network.

today: RFC 9037 is an Informational RFC published in June 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the reference for how to implement DetNet MPLS over IEEE 802.1 TSN bridged networks.

sections.title: Why DetNet and TSN Together
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) is a service offered by a network to ensure that certain flows receive low packet loss and guaranteed maximum latency from end to end. It splits the work into a service layer (that protects and reorders traffic) and a forwarding layer (that allocates resources and routes explicitly).

DetNet uses MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) for the data plane. MPLS is a forwarding technology that uses short labels rather than long IP addresses to make fast routing decisions. IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) is a separate standard for Layer 2 bridged networks that provides similar guarantees: zero congestion loss and bounded latency.

This document does not define new protocols. Instead, it shows how to map DetNet MPLS flows to TSN streams so the two technologies can work together, letting network operators build paths where MPLS routers are connected by TSN bridges.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet over MPLS is a way to guarantee fast delivery through routers. TSN is a way to guarantee fast delivery through bridges. This RFC explains how to use both at the same time.

sections.title: How the Two Layers Work
sections.content:
A DetNet MPLS node operates in two layers. The service sub-layer handles DetNet-specific work: it uses the service label (S-Label) to identify flows and apply replication, elimination, and reordering functions (PREOF). The forwarding sub-layer handles resource allocation and explicit routes, using forwarding labels (F-Labels) that work with MPLS Traffic Engineering.

Edge and relay nodes understand both layers and add or remove labels as needed. Transit nodes inside the network only handle the forwarding layer. When MPLS nodes are connected by a TSN sub-network, the sub-network acts as a single hop from the MPLS perspective, and the nodes at its edges become both Talkers (senders) and Listeners (receivers) in TSN terms.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it like mail: one layer handles which postal zone, and another layer handles getting your specific letter to your house. When you cross a TSN bridge, the bridge becomes responsible for that middle leg.

sections.title: Mapping Flows to TSN Streams
sections.content:
To send a DetNet MPLS flow through a TSN sub-network, the MPLS nodes must identify which DetNet flows map to which TSN streams. This is done using frame-level identification: a passive stream identification function catches the MPLS labels, and an active stream identification function changes the Ethernet header fields (destination MAC, VLAN-ID, and priority) to mark the flow for TSN processing.

The RFC recommends the Mask-and-Match stream identification function (from IEEE 802.1CBdb) for passive identification, and the Active Destination MAC and VLAN function (from IEEE 802.1CB) for active identification. Together these allow DetNet flows to be translated into TSN Stream IDs, and they can be reversed on the far side to restore the original Ethernet addressing.
sections.plainLanguage: You write your flow's MPLS label on the envelope, and the bridge reads that to figure out how to handle it inside the TSN network.

sections.title: TSN-Aware and TSN-Unaware Nodes
sections.content:
A TSN-aware MPLS (DetNet) node understands TSN and can add the right Ethernet headers for TSN processing. It must support the TSN stream identification functions, the sequencing and sequence encode/decode functions, and the frame replication and elimination (FRER) functions defined in IEEE 802.1CB. This includes support for the Redundancy tag (R-TAG) format.

A TSN-unaware MPLS (DetNet) node does not speak TSN. The TSN relay nodes at the edges of the sub-network must do the translation work for it. The RFC places no requirements on TSN-unaware nodes themselves; all the work falls to the network at the boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: Smart MPLS nodes that understand TSN can put the right labels on their packets before handing them to the bridge. Dumb nodes just send packets and let the bridge figure it out.

sections.title: Management and Control Challenges
sections.content:
Configuring DetNet MPLS over TSN requires information from both worlds: DetNet MPLS configuration (labels, routes), TSN configuration (stream identification, QoS parameters), and the mapping between them. This mapping must be provisioned per DetNet flow, and DetNet flow parameters (like per-hop delay) may differ from TSN parameters because the TSN sub-network is just one hop in the end-to-end path.

Converting DetNet identifiers to TSN identifiers is a major challenge. Determining the right next-hop destination and which interface it connects to can be non-obvious when dealing with mesh networks. Additionally, TSN-specific functions (like FRER configuration) are domain-specific decisions that may not be visible in the DetNet control plane. The document notes that service protection interworking between DetNet's PREOF and TSN's FRER is left for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: Making the two systems talk requires knowing both routing languages and translating between them. It is complicated, but possible.
